notes: Thursday 12 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Wed 11 Nov. Economy: Goolsbee calls inflation 'borderline disturbing'; US gas under $4; Canada envoy warns on tariffs; October retail sales slowest in a year. Tech: WSJ says Nvidia board preparing to oust Jensen Huang; CoreWeave +24%; AI data centers plan on-site gas power; DOJ sues Lyft over disability refusals. Politics: Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat; Russia-Ukraine prisoner swap; Bessent moves to military base; Indonesia VP Gibran resigns. Literature (US): Elordi to star in The Executioner's Song; Nancy Isenberg on nepo babies; Tom Drury's West of Loveland; Conrad-Pérez on modern New York. Society: Spain general strike on housing; Saudi lashing sentence for Kenyan mother; Gaza storm tents; US measles elimination status at risk.

stories.headline: Fed's Goolsbee calls US inflation 'borderline disturbing' as bigger rate hikes come into view
stories.dek: October prices rose 0.4%, the third hot month in a row. Some Fed officials now openly talk about a half-point hike in December.
stories.caveman: Inflation means prices going up. The US government said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October alone, more than experts expected, and the third month in a row of big jumps. Austan Goolsbee, who runs the Chicago branch of the Federal Reserve, told PBS it was 'another distressing report — borderline disturbing.' He said price pressure from tariffs has not faded the way he hoped, and prices for services stay high. The Fed fights inflation by raising interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive and slows spending. It usually moves by a quarter point. But Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot report could push him to back a bigger half-point hike in December. Dallas Fed chief Lorie Logan wants two more quarter-point hikes. Philadelphia Fed chief Anna Paulson said slower, gradual steps are enough for now. The Fed's rate now sits at 3.75%–4%.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher rates mean pricier mortgages, car loans and credit cards. They can cool prices but also slow hiring. What the Fed does in December ripples into world markets, including Taiwan stocks.
stories.camps: Hawks say act fast before people start expecting high inflation forever. Doves worry big hikes could tip the economy into a slump. Critics of the White House point to tariffs as a key cause; the administration says tariffs protect US workers.
stories.image_alt: Federal Reserve official at an economics conference (CNBC file photo accompanying the story)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: The US central bank. It sets the main interest rate to keep prices and jobs steady.
Consumer price index: a measure of how much a basket of everyday goods and services costs.
When the central bank raises interest rates to slow borrowing and cool prices.
An official who wants tougher action against inflation. A dove prefers a gentler approach.

stories.headline: US gas drops below $4 a gallon for the first time in months
stories.dek: The national average is now $3.94, down about 40 cents in a month. Cheaper crude oil is the main reason, but a flare-up in the Iran war could reverse it.
stories.caveman: Gasoline is the fuel most American cars use. According to AAA, the average price fell under $4 a gallon on Tuesday and is now $3.94 — about 40 cents cheaper than a month ago. Part of the drop is normal for autumn: fewer people drive, refineries finish yearly repairs, and the cheaper 'winter blend' of gas goes on sale. But the biggest reason, says analyst Jorge León of Rystad Energy, is that Brent crude oil has fallen to about $90 a barrel. More Middle East oil is moving by pipeline, and traders are cheered by US–Iran diplomacy. León warns that if the war escalates — for example if President Trump uses military action to gain leverage before Democrats take over Congress in January — much of that drop could vanish fast.
stories.why_it_matters: Gas prices hit every family budget and feed into inflation. Cheaper fuel helps, but the relief depends on a war far away.
stories.camps: Some will credit diplomacy for lower prices. Analysts say seasons and oil markets matter more than politics. Democrats in Congress want to end the war and could use their budget power to push for it.
stories.image_alt: A gas pump nozzle in a car in Austin, Texas
stories.image_credit: Photo: Brandon Bell/Getty Images via NPR

terms.explain: A main world benchmark price for oil, used to price much of the oil sold globally.
A big US motoring club that tracks average gas prices.
A cheaper type of gasoline sold in cold months; it helps engines start in freezing weather.

stories.headline: Canada's ambassador: Trump tariffs raise costs and scare off investment in the US
stories.dek: Mark Wiseman says uncertainty makes companies slower to build plants. A New York Fed study found nearly 90% of tariff costs land on US importers.
stories.caveman: A tariff is a tax on goods coming from another country. Canada's ambassador to the US, Mark Wiseman, told a big business meeting in Washington that President Trump's tariffs make it more expensive and riskier for companies to invest. 'Uncertainty increases your cost of capital,' he said — if firms don't know the rules, they wait before building factories or spending on research. The US and Canada traded about $570 billion in goods in the first nine months of 2026, less than in the same months of 2022–2024. US duties on Canadian goods jumped from $400 million in 2024 to $10 billion in 2025. A New York Fed study found almost 90% of tariff costs are paid by US importers, and about a quarter eventually shows up in shop prices, with more price pressure expected in 2027. Trump says tariffs protect American factories and workers and accuses Canada of unfair trade.
stories.why_it_matters: Canada is one of America's biggest trading partners. Tariff fights between them affect prices, jobs and supply chains well beyond North America.
stories.camps: The White House says tariffs bring jobs home and pressure unfair partners. Canada and many economists say they act like a tax on American shoppers and companies, and the uncertainty chills investment.
stories.image_alt: CNBC photo accompanying its report on US–Canada tariffs
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A tax a country puts on goods imported from another country.
How expensive it is for a company to get money to invest. Risk makes it higher.
A business that buys goods from another country to sell or use at home.

stories.headline: US shoppers keep spending but show strain: October retail sales grow at slowest pace in nearly a year
stories.dek: Retail spending rose just 0.2% from September. Electronics jumped as AI-driven memory chip costs pushed up gadget prices; furniture slipped.
stories.caveman: Retail sales means money people spend in shops and online. The CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor, built from about 120 million debit and credit cards, says Americans spent $561.7 billion in October — only 0.2% more than in September, the smallest monthly rise since November 2025. Compared with a year ago, spending was up 3.6%. Halloween and early holiday deals kept the number from being weaker. The National Retail Federation's boss, Matthew Shay, said families are budgeting carefully and waiting for sales. Electronics spending rose 9.3% over a year, partly because companies raised prices on things like MacBooks and Xboxes as AI demand made memory chips more expensive. Furniture spending fell, hurt by a frozen housing market and higher mortgage rates.
stories.why_it_matters: Consumer spending drives about two-thirds of the US economy. If shoppers pull back, companies sell less — including Asian firms that make the gadgets.
stories.camps: Retailers say deals keep shoppers coming. Some economists see a slow cooling, not a crash. Others warn high prices and rising rates are squeezing lower-income families hardest.
stories.image_alt: A shopper in a US store aisle
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Total money people spend buying goods in stores and online.
National Retail Federation, the main trade group for US retailers.
Numbers changed to remove normal yearly patterns, like holiday shopping, so months can be compared fairly.

stories.headline: Nvidia board reportedly prepares to oust CEO Jensen Huang; stock falls 9% after hours
stories.dek: The Wall Street Journal says the board may meet to decide his future. The New York Times reported a second affair, with a senior Nvidia executive.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI. Its famous boss, Jensen Huang, already admitted last week to an affair with a woman US intelligence officials believe spies for China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him. Minutes later, The Wall Street Journal reported the board is preparing to remove him and could meet as soon as Wednesday. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in after-hours trading. Nvidia and Powell did not immediately comment. Huang had written to staff: 'I was unfaithful to my wife... There is no excuse for what I did.' Nvidia stock was already on track for a sixth straight weekly drop amid worries about the AI boom.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the world's most important AI company and a giant customer of Taiwan's TSMC and many Taiwanese suppliers. A leadership crisis there shakes markets everywhere.
stories.camps: Governance experts say a CEO dating a subordinate and a suspected spy is a serious breach and the board must act. Supporters say Huang built Nvidia and replacing him is risky. Lawmakers on both sides focus on the national security angle and China chip exports.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaking at a tech event in Paris
stories.image_credit: Photo: Reuters via CNBC

terms.explain: To force someone out of their job.
The group of directors who oversee a company and can hire or fire the CEO.
Buying and selling stocks after the main market closes at 4pm New York time.
China's main spy agency.

stories.headline: CoreWeave soars 24% after strong earnings, easing fears about AI cloud debt
stories.dek: The AI cloud renter's revenue jumped 168% to $3.7 billion. Its CEO says demand for 2027 capacity is '10x oversubscribed.'
stories.caveman: CoreWeave is a 'neocloud' — a company that rents out huge rooms of Nvidia AI chips to firms like OpenAI. Investors had grown nervous because CoreWeave borrowed a lot of money to build data centers, and the price of insuring its debt against default jumped to distress levels. Then on Tuesday it reported third-quarter revenue up 168% to $3.7 billion, beat forecasts, and raised its outlook. On Wednesday the stock jumped 24.7%, its best day since April 2025. CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC demand 'is and remains overwhelming' and that the capacity left for 2027 is 10 times oversubscribed. He said the company will soon sell more debt backed by its data center assets at about 7%–7.5% interest, and that about $9 billion in customer prepayments also helps fund growth. He also canceled his own planned share sales.
stories.why_it_matters: CoreWeave is a test of whether the AI building boom can pay its bills. Good news here lifted Asian tech stocks, including in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Bulls say this proves AI demand is real. Skeptics note the company still carries heavy debt, depends on a few big customers, and could suffer if AI spending slows.
stories.image_alt: CoreWeave signage on its stock market debut day
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: A newer cloud company that mainly rents AI computing power, unlike giants such as Amazon or Microsoft.
More customers want something than there is supply.
A kind of insurance investors buy against a company failing to repay debt. A higher price means more fear.
A company's own forecast of future sales or profit.

stories.headline: AI data centers plan their own gas power plants on a huge scale, research finds
stories.dek: BloombergNEF counts 181GW of planned on-site gas power, 90% of it in the US — close to four times Britain's peak electricity demand.
stories.caveman: AI data centers need enormous amounts of electricity. Waiting years to connect to the public power grid is too slow for some builders, so many plan to put their own gas-fired power stations right on site. Research from BloombergNEF found plans for 181 gigawatts of this gas power across the US, UK and Europe — almost four times Great Britain's total peak demand. About 90% is planned in the US. If built, the US plants alone would emit about 345 million tonnes of greenhouse gases a year, roughly like 72.8 million gasoline cars. The report says AI data center electricity use could almost quadruple by 2035 to about 7% of world demand. Climate campaigners say these 'temporary' plants could lock in pollution for years. The report landed as world leaders met at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey.
stories.why_it_matters: The AI race is colliding with climate goals. Whether data centers run on gas or clean power will shape emissions for decades — and Taiwan faces its own electricity squeeze from chip and AI growth.
stories.camps: Tech companies say speed matters and gas is a bridge until grids catch up. Environmental groups say it's a climate step backward and want clean power and faster grid upgrades instead.
stories.image_alt: Gas-fired power infrastructure of the kind planned at data center sites
stories.image_credit: Photo: Anton Gvozdikov/Alamy via The Guardian

terms.explain: A building full of computers (servers) that run websites, apps and AI.
A unit of power: one billion watts. One GW can power hundreds of thousands of homes.
The network of power lines that carries electricity from power plants to users.
The 31st yearly UN climate summit, held this year in Turkey.

stories.headline: US Justice Department sues Lyft, saying drivers refuse riders with wheelchairs and guide dogs
stories.dek: The lawsuit says Lyft knew about widespread disability discrimination and failed to stop it. Lyft firmly rejects the claims.
stories.caveman: Lyft is a ride-hailing app, like Uber. The US Justice Department sued Lyft in federal court in California, saying its drivers often refuse to take people who use wheelchairs or need service animals. That would break the Americans with Disabilities Act, a 1990 law that bans discrimination against disabled people. The complaint gives examples: a Nevada woman in a wheelchair says a driver drove away while she waved; a Texas man with vision and hearing loss began leaving his guide dog at home to avoid being turned down. The government says Lyft knew about 'widespread' discrimination but didn't act. Lyft firmly denies it and says its rules require drivers to follow the law. The government filed a similar case against Uber last year, still ongoing.
stories.why_it_matters: Disabled people depend on ride apps to get to work, doctors and daily life. The case tests how much responsibility tech platforms have for what their gig drivers do.
stories.camps: Disability advocates say apps profit from drivers and must enforce the rules. Lyft says it already requires accommodation and punishes refusals. Some see a wider fight over who is responsible in the gig economy.
stories.image_alt: A Lyft-branded car on a US street
stories.image_credit: Photo: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Americans with Disabilities Act: a US law that bans discrimination against disabled people in jobs, transport and public places.
A trained animal, often a dog, that helps a disabled person, such as guiding someone who is blind.
Work done as short jobs through apps, like ride-hailing or food delivery.

stories.headline: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat in stunning upset
stories.dek: He beat Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith after more than a week of counting, becoming the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction.
stories.caveman: Mississippi is one of America's most Republican states. It had not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1982, or a Black senator since the 1870s. After more than a week of counting, Democrat Scott Colom beat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He took a narrow lead on election night that grew as provisional ballots were counted. Colom, a seventh-generation Mississippian, became the first Black district attorney in his area in 2015. The Guardian says his win capped a national wave of anger at the Trump administration, and that voters in the South were also stirred up by efforts to redraw Black-majority voting districts. The last Black senator from Mississippi, Blanche K Bruce, was born into slavery.
stories.why_it_matters: Every Senate seat matters for which party controls laws and appointments. A Democratic win in deep-red Mississippi shows how big the 2026 midterm swing was.
stories.camps: Democrats call it proof that their message reaches beyond cities. Republicans point to a weak national mood and local factors. Analysts say Colom's moderate, local profile helped.
stories.image_alt: Scott Colom in Jackson, Mississippi, on 3 November 2026
stories.image_credit: Photo: Eric Shelton/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: When the person expected to lose wins.
The period after the US Civil War (1865–1877) when formerly enslaved Black men briefly won office in the South.
A vote set aside to be checked later, for example when a voter's registration is unclear.
The person who already holds the job.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine agree to biggest prisoner swap of the war, but no peace breakthrough
stories.dek: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff led two days of talks in Abu Dhabi. They head to Moscow to see Putin, then to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy.
stories.caveman: Russia invaded Ukraine almost five years ago. This week the two sides held their first US-brokered talks since February, in Abu Dhabi. They agreed on what they called the war's largest prisoner exchange — more than 1,000 prisoners from each side are expected. But they made little progress on ending the war. A Ukrainian negotiator said Russia arrived with 'very, very strict directives,' though he saw 'really big progress' on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war and hoped for a deal before the new year. Kushner said he sees 'all the different ingredients to make a deal.' The US envoys will brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and then meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European partners in Dublin.
stories.why_it_matters: The war shapes energy prices, food supply and security across Europe and beyond. A prisoner swap brings families relief even without peace.
stories.camps: Ukraine says it won't give up land cheaply — Zelenskyy said Ukraine is 'not real estate.' Russia wants big concessions. Some in Europe worry a rushed US-led deal could reward the invasion.
stories.image_alt: Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence service, speaks after talks in Abu Dhabi
stories.image_credit: Photo: Altaf Qadri/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: When two sides at war swap captured soldiers or civilians.
A person sent to represent a government in talks.
Promises from other countries to help protect Ukraine if it is attacked again.

stories.headline: US Treasury Secretary Bessent moves to a military base over Iranian threats
stories.dek: Officials say Iran's plots against US targets have become more advanced. Three Iranians were indicted over nearly 20 attacks and attempts in Europe and the US.
stories.caveman: The US and Iran are in an uneasy war, with on-and-off fighting. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent leads 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a campaign of sanctions to choke Iran's economy, which has made him a top target, according to The New York Times. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC he moved from his Washington home to a military base for safety, partly because a past newspaper photo let people locate his house. A Treasury spokesperson said he 'will not be deterred.' Separately, the Justice Department said three Iranian nationals were charged with terrorism over nearly 20 attacks and attempts in Europe and the US, including a September attack on RAF Fairford, a British base where US troops are stationed. Bessent is reportedly the latest Trump official to move onto a base.
stories.why_it_matters: When a top economic official needs military protection, it shows how dangerous the US–Iran conflict has become — and it affects oil prices and markets worldwide.
stories.camps: The administration says sanctions and the blockade are working. Critics say the war is risky and costly; most Americans in a recent Reuters poll want the new Congress to end it.
stories.image_alt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking at a podium
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Penalties, like bans on trade or freezing money, used to pressure a country.
Formally charged with a crime by a grand jury.
The US cabinet member in charge of government money, taxes and financial sanctions.

stories.headline: Indonesia's vice president Gibran resigns after court rules his school document invalid
stories.dek: Gibran, son of ex-president Jokowi, faced an impeachment push. His exit could strain the alliance that put President Prabowo in power.
stories.caveman: Gibran Rakabuming Raka became Indonesia's vice president in 2024, at 36, after a controversial court ruling let him run. He is the son of former president Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi. Indonesian law says a vice president must have finished high school or equal. Gibran studied in Singapore and Australia and used an Indonesian 'equivalence' certificate. Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that document invalid, saying there was no proof he had a foreign diploma that matched high school. More than 100 lawmakers then backed a move that could lead to impeachment. An aide told the BBC Gibran handed his resignation letter to President Prabowo Subianto on Wednesday; it is unclear if it has been accepted. Gibran had asked for a chance to prove his credentials.
stories.why_it_matters: Indonesia is the world's third-largest democracy and a big Southeast Asian economy. A political shake-up there matters for the region, including Taiwan's trade and migrant worker ties.
stories.camps: Critics say the case shows family dynasties bending rules. Gibran's backers say university study proves he finished high school. Analysts watch whether the Prabowo–Jokowi alliance breaks apart.
stories.image_alt: Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images via BBC

terms.explain: To formally accuse a top official, which can lead to removing them from office.
A family that holds power across generations.
A document saying a foreign qualification equals a local one.

stories.headline: HOT: Jacob Elordi to star in and produce a new take on Norman Mailer's 'The Executioner's Song'
stories.dek: Fresh off playing the Creature in Frankenstein, Elordi is taking on Mailer's Pulitzer-winning 1979 book about killer Gary Gilmore.
stories.caveman: Norman Mailer was a giant of American writing. His nearly 1,000-page 'The Executioner's Song' tells the true story of Gary Gilmore, who murdered two men in Utah in 1976 and then demanded to be executed, at a time when the death penalty was on hold across the US. He was shot by firing squad in 1977. Mailer wrote it in plain, flat sentences, like a novel built from real interviews, many gathered by photographer Lawrence Schiller. Joan Didion called it 'an absolutely astonishing book.' Now Australian actor Jacob Elordi, Oscar-nominated for playing the Creature in 'Frankenstein,' will star and, for the first time, produce. Scott Stuber of United Artists is among the producers, and Schiller, who directed a 1982 film version with Tommy Lee Jones, will executive-produce.
stories.why_it_matters: When a hot young star picks an old classic, sales and readers usually follow. It puts big questions — the death penalty, violence and media frenzy — back in pop culture.
stories.camps: Fans of the book are curious whether a new version can match its quiet power. Some critics question whether retelling a killer's story glamorizes him; others say it's essential American history.
stories.image_alt: Cover art for Norman Mailer's The Executioner's Song
stories.image_credit: Photo: Literary Hub

terms.explain: A film or TV version made from a book.
A top US award for writing and journalism.
When the state kills a person as punishment for a crime.
A senior producer, often giving rights, money or advice rather than daily work.

stories.headline: HOT: Nancy Isenberg's new book takes aim at America's 'nepo babies'
stories.dek: An excerpt from 'Aristocracy, American Style' argues Americans quietly accept inherited privilege — in Hollywood, news, publishing and politics.
stories.caveman: A 'nepo baby' is someone who got ahead partly because a parent was already famous or powerful. Historian Nancy Isenberg, known for her bestseller 'White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America,' has a new book, 'Aristocracy, American Style' (Viking). In an excerpt on Literary Hub, she argues that Americans like to think their country has no aristocracy, yet they happily accept nepotism. She lists Hollywood families from the Barrymores to the Fondas and Douglases, TV news figures whose parents were famous anchors or politicians, and families that pass down businesses and newspapers. Her point: talent may be real, but these people never had to compete with the crowd from the bottom, and that keeps power inside the same circles.
stories.why_it_matters: It turns a viral internet joke into a serious question about class and fairness — a hot topic as Americans argue about inequality and who gets opportunities.
stories.camps: Some readers will cheer the takedown of inherited privilege. Others argue that family connections exist everywhere and many heirs still work hard and earn their place.
stories.image_alt: Illustration accompanying the Literary Hub excerpt on political nepo babies
stories.image_credit: Photo: Literary Hub

terms.explain: Short for nepotism baby: a child of famous or powerful parents who benefits from that connection.
Favoring your relatives when giving jobs or chances.
A class of people who hold power and status mainly through birth and family.
A short section taken from a longer book.

stories.headline: Tom Drury on 'flown-over country' as his new Iowa novel 'West of Loveland' arrives
stories.dek: The cult-favorite novelist says writers should see the Midwest from the ground, not from the airplane window.
stories.caveman: Coastal Americans sometimes call the middle of the country 'flyover country' — places they only see from a plane. Novelist Tom Drury, who grew up in an Iowa town of about 200 people surrounded by corn and soybean farms, wants to flip that. In a talk now published by Literary Hub, he suggests 'flownover country,' centered on the people below. The talk came from a 2022 conference in Austria about how 'flyover' became a symbol of cultural ranking and political division. His short story for that project, about a teenage boy and his aunt who find a gun by the road, became the first chapter of his new novel, 'West of Loveland' (Grove Press). Drury, who lives in Iowa City, is admired for 'The End of Vandalism' and the National Book Award-longlisted 'Pacific.'
stories.why_it_matters: Who gets to tell stories about rural America matters, especially after elections that split city and country. Drury is a writer's writer whose new books are an event for fans.
stories.camps: Readers who love quiet, funny small-town fiction will be excited. Some argue 'flyover' talk is overblown; others say coastal culture still ignores rural lives.
stories.image_alt: An Iowa cornfield
stories.image_credit: Photo: Literary Hub

terms.explain: A sometimes mocking name for the middle of the US, which coastal travelers fly over.
The first, longer list of books chosen for a prize, before the shortlist and winner.
The north-central part of the US, including Iowa, known for farming.

stories.headline: David Conrad-Pérez picks 10 books on the people who really built modern New York
stories.dek: The author of a new Triangle Shirtwaist Fire history says the city's workers, tenants and organizers deserve as much attention as its millionaires.
stories.caveman: New York loves naming buildings after rich builders and bankers. Historian David Conrad-Pérez, author of 'Fire in the Heart of the City: The Triangle Shirtwaist Fire and the Origins of Modern Charity' (NYU Press), argues the people who dug the tunnels, kept the lights on and set the tables — like his own ancestors who were domestic workers — matter just as much. For Literary Hub he recommends 10 books about the birth of modern New York. He warns that archives are not neutral: rich families leave big piles of letters, while workers' lives survive only in scraps, so historians must not confuse a thick paper trail with the whole story. The 1911 Triangle fire killed 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women, and led to new safety laws.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a reading list for anyone curious about labor, immigration and who gets remembered — themes that still shape New York politics today.
stories.camps: Labor historians will welcome the focus on workers. Others say the city's famous builders and philanthropists still deserve credit for what they made possible.
stories.image_alt: A view of New York City
stories.image_credit: Photo: Literary Hub

terms.explain: A 1911 factory fire in New York that killed 146 garment workers and led to major worker safety laws.
A collection of old records, letters and papers kept for history.
Giving money to help causes or the public.

stories.headline: Millions join Spain's first general strike in 14 years over sky-high housing costs
stories.dek: Tenants' groups called the 24-hour stoppage, later backed by unions. Barcelona saw roadblocks, burning tyres and clashes ahead of an election.
stories.caveman: A general strike is when workers across many jobs stop work on the same day. On Wednesday, Spain had its first in 14 years. Unusually, it was called by tenants' associations — groups of renters — angry that rents and home prices have soared. Unions joined. The tenants' confederation said about 4 million people took part by midday. Unions reported 90% participation in car factories and ports and 82% in waste collection, strongest in Catalonia and Andalucía. Many schools and universities closed or ran at minimum. In Barcelona, pickets set up roadblocks, some with burning tyres, public transport nearly stopped and some protesters clashed with police. 'We, the workers... are the ones with the power to halt production,' said Sandra Mora of the Madrid Tenants' Union. The strike comes just before an election in which the far right could gain power.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing costs are a crisis in many cities, from Madrid to Taipei. Spain shows renters organizing like workers to demand change.
stories.camps: Strikers want rent controls and more public housing. Businesses and some politicians say strikes hurt the economy and that more building, not limits, is the fix. The far right blames immigration, which critics call scapegoating.
stories.image_alt: Protesters take to the streets in Valencia during the general strike
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ana Escobar/EPA via The Guardian

terms.explain: When workers across many industries stop work together to protest.
A group of renters who organize to protect their rights against landlords.
Strikers standing outside workplaces to stop people going in.
Political groups with very strong nationalist and anti-immigration views.

stories.headline: Kenyan domestic worker in Saudi Arabia reportedly sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage
stories.dek: Rights groups call it an act of violence and say women migrant workers are targeted. A UN expert's planned visit to Saudi Arabia was postponed.
stories.caveman: In Saudi Arabia, sex outside marriage is a crime under its sharia legal system. Esther Wanja Muthoni, a Kenyan woman who went there to work as a housekeeper and nanny, reportedly became pregnant during a short relationship with an Egyptian man who later left the country. Because she gave birth in a hospital, and hospitals must report unmarried mothers, the case reached the authorities. Last month she was reportedly sentenced to 100 lashes. 'I don't deserve this,' she told The New York Times. Rights groups say women are punished far more than men, and many migrant women give birth at home to avoid being reported. ALQST, a Saudi rights group, called the ruling an act of violence. The UN special rapporteur on violence against women, Reem Alsalem, says she will raise such cases after her planned visit was postponed.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of women from Africa and Asia work in Gulf homes, often with few protections. This case shows how laws on morality can fall hardest on the poorest women.
stories.camps: Human rights groups demand the sentence be dropped and migrant workers protected. Saudi authorities say they apply their own laws. Kenya faces pressure to protect citizens it sends abroad.
stories.image_alt: The Riyadh skyline in Saudi Arabia
stories.image_credit: Photo: Hasan Zaidi/Alamy via The Guardian

stories.headline: Storms flood Gaza tents as 150,000 new shelters wait outside for Israeli approval
stories.dek: At least four children and a woman died in weekend storms. Aid groups fear hypothermia and disease as winter sets in.
stories.caveman: Most people in Gaza lost their homes in the war and now live in tents. Weekend storms with heavy rain and wind tore and flooded many of them. At least four Palestinian children and a woman were killed. Sewage spilled into tents. 'My kids are all sick,' said Raed Jamal, a displaced father who used pots all night to catch rain leaking through his roof. Aid agencies say 150,000 new shelters are sitting outside Gaza waiting for Israel to approve their entry. The UN says 940,000 people live in makeshift tents in areas at risk of flooding. Medical Aid for Palestinians fears more breathing illnesses and more children dying of cold, as happened last winter.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter can be as deadly as bombs for families with no real shelter. Getting tents and heating in is a matter of life and death.
stories.camps: Aid groups say Israel is slowing vital supplies. Israel generally says it inspects goods for security and blames Hamas and distribution problems. Many governments urge faster access.

stories.headline: US could lose its "measles eliminated" status amid worst outbreak since 1991
stories.dek: More than 5,400 cases and multiple child deaths this year. Experts blame falling vaccination rates and Health Secretary RFK Jr's vaccine policies.
stories.caveman: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases on Earth. A country is called 'measles eliminated' when the virus no longer spreads inside it all year. The US won that status in 2000. Now a panel of eight experts for the Pan American Health Organization, part of the WHO, is reviewing whether the US has lost it, with the PAHO director making the final call. The US has more than 5,400 cases this year, its worst since 1991, according to a Johns Hopkins tracker. Six people died in Pennsylvania, a child died in New York on election day, and an infant died in Wisconsin. Nearly every state has an outbreak. Vaccine expert Dr Paul Offit, a critic of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, called it 'a tremendous step backwards' and said measles is now endemic.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles can kill children and cause brain damage. It is easily prevented by vaccines, so losing control shows how trust in vaccines affects public health.
stories.camps: Doctors and public health experts blame lower vaccination and RFK Jr's vaccine skepticism. Kennedy and his supporters frame their policies as medical freedom and choice. Most Americans still vaccinate their children.
